utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. May I start by calling for the appearances, please. 11 MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Di Fazio. I appear for the Prosecution together with our -- Yes. Yes, I must say, if Your Honours, please, just before I do the announcements, I'm getting French on number 4. Well, it may improve my French, but I can't have that today. Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Di Fazio. I appear for the Prosecution together with our case manager, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just to brush up my learned friend's French [Interpretation] Good morning, good morning, Judges. Today appearing for Mr. Zupljanin, for the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin, counsel Igor Pantelic; counsel Dragan Krgovic; and our associate Mr. Eric Tully; and a charming young lady as our case manager, mademoiselle Katarina Danicic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the witness returned to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have some preliminaries. Can we go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, good morning to you. I would remind you that you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Majkic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the role and the relationship of the police with the public prosecutor's office and the justice system, that is, the regular judge in those procedures that were in place. Would you agree with me if I say that the police in fact was a technical service of the public prosecutor's office in the so-called pre-indictment proceedings and that it acted on the instructions of the public prosecutor's office in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure as to what pre-indictment actions to take?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And certainly, in certain stages the police also acted on the instructions of the investigative judge who led this investigation proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you would agree that for all practical purposes the public prosecutor's office was the body which led pre-indictment proceedings, made motions and requests for the implementation of investigative procedures, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the police was practically duty-bound to act on the instructions of the public prosecutor and the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the job of the police was to work to try to detect perpetrators of crimes using its own methods, using informers, collecting information, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we now go through a part of your statement, the one that you gave to the Prosecution in 2001 and 2008. I have a copy for you in Serbian language to facilitate communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is -- [Interpretation] The B/C/S version is 65 ter 9003, and may I ask the usher to kindly put it before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. Majkic, would you agree with me that practically the powers of police officers are based on the Law on Criminal -- Law on Internal Affairs, not on orders from above; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we have both versions. Look at paragraph 19, please. In English it's page 4 and in B/C/S it's page 6, paragraph 19. So in this statement you mention that in 1941 around 5.000 Serbs had been killed in Sanski Most. Would you explain to us very briefly, because this is not the subject of these proceedings, what is this all about? Why did you mention this historical detail or just explain briefly what happened in 1941.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened some time in the month of July. The servants of the Ustashas and the Ustasha units in Sanski Most were rounding up people from 14 to 70 years of age from all the villages where Serbs lived and brought them into depots and warehouses in town and locked them up. From the 1st until the 3rd of August, around 5.000 of them were killed at a cemetery now called Susnjar, where today there is a monument to the victims of Ustasha terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Those were in fact the forces of the Muslim Handzar division cooperating with the forces of the Ustasha regime. They committed these crimes in your area; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1992, although this was not directly referred to, there must have been great concern and anxiety among the Serbs about what was going to follow, especially knowing that there were already Serbian casualties and victims in the neighbouring territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you now turn to page -- to the page of your statement where paragraph 34 begins. In English it's 7, in B/C/S it's 10. We discussed the subject of this paragraph yesterday, but I would like you to give me a summarised version and conclusion. Here you say that the chief of a police station is the one who coordinates the work of all these sectors and that at that time, when you took over as chief of police station, there were around 100 people working in the Sanski Most police station.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, out of those 100, if I remember well from looking at that list, I believe that at least 30 were clerks, typists, administrative workers, couriers, the cleaning personnel; in other words, not active-duty policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we employed 25 to 30 per cent of such personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding this fact, we know from various testimonies and from the fact of this case that this group, SOS, led by a certain Njunja had very serious weaponry. They even had some sort of three-barrelled gun. They were seasoned fighters. Tell me, if you were to compare the strength of the uniformed police in Sanski Most with that SOS group, if an armed conflict occurred between them, what would be the outcome? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, there's an assumption in there that the witness hasn't testified about. Yesterday his evidence was he thought they were local lads - Friday and yesterday - local lads, seven to eight, seven to eight of them. And he said later - and he never clarified this - he found out there were more. Now, the assumption in the question is that there are more and that they're well armed. So the reality of what -- the reality of the strength and numbers of the SOS hasn't yet been made clear, but the assumption is that -- in the question is that the police couldn't cope with it, whatever that might have been, and we don't know. The only definite thing we have so far is seven to eight local lads, and later he found out there were more. That's my recollection of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe my learned friend -- MR. DI FAZIO: So that should be -- that should be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe my learned friend was away from the office when we discussed these matters. Maybe he's not so familiar with his own case and the evidence, but we know, Your Honours, what was the numbers of SOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I might -- Mr. Di Fazio, I was about to say that the thrust of your objection is that it -- I think the expression goes assumes facts not in evidence. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And that is not -- and that's the intervention Mr. Pantelic is now making. That's not entirely correct, it may not be in evidence out of the mouth of this witness, but in terms of the body of the evidence, I don't know that it is an objection which the way you have phrased it stands. Perhaps the concern could be addressed by Mr. Pantelic, refining the question to bring it home to this witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. All right. Well -- very well, Your Honours. But if that is the case, then you, as you listen to this evidence, should know exactly what the comparison is -- what -- the comparison that's being made. Mr. Pantelic -- the thrust of Mr. Pantelic's question is that the numbers of police in Sanski Most with their weaponry were in no position to deal with the SOS. But we still don't know what this witness's position on the strength of the SOS was at different times. So if he says "yes" or answers "yes," what do you know, what meaning does his evidence carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a problem with this. I will ask witness of his personal knowledge of that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Majkic, why don't you describe now to the Trial Chamber what you knew about the strength of that armed group, the SOS in Sanski Most in 1992. Briefly explain how many of them there were, what kind of weapons they had, all you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have been saying in my evidence the past few days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what this witness knew at the moment he was chief of police or at any moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Majkic, we know from your evidence that you had certain knowledge in end 1991, in the beginning of 1992 about this armed formation. But since you were in Sanski Most throughout 1992, which covers the period of this indictment, tell the Trial Chamber from the moment you found out about that SOS group until the end of 1992 what was your personal knowledge about the strength of that unit we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have been saying in my evidence the past few days, we in the police practically knew next to nothing about them. We got this information from the citizenry, from the people. The people started talking about the SOS and who might be in it. We in the police would see them in groups of seven to eight. We had an idea who the leaders were of this paramilitary unit, but they were in this group of seven or eight when they were home. When they would go out to war, we didn't see them anymore. We had no idea of their organisation. Even worse, we didn't know anything about them. If we had known that there were seven or eight, we would have dealt with them easily; but what if there were more than seven or eight, what then? That's one. And second, these were soldiers that had been in the battle-field for ten months, ever since 1991 in the summer. We would see them only when they would come on leave to Sanski Most. There was also military police in Prijedor and it also toured and inspected Sanski Most. They kept them under surveillance and monitoring. So I had no reason to go and interview them, for instance, about these bombings and explosives that had been set in various incidents because we never succeeded in establishing that it was them, and their behaviour in everyday life did not give us any cause to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something. When you ceased being chief of police, did you know -- did you learn at that point that within their unit they had a sort of a three-barrelled gun?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it on a number of occasions when they transported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know that some threats were made to some judicial officers for putting Serbs on trial, were there any protests made by SOS members? Did you hear of any such incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you know that they acted within the 6th Krajina Brigade and that they were under the command of Colonel Basara at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that they were soldiers of the 6th Krajina at the time, and we knew when they were out on the front; when they were not at the front, we would see them in Sanski Most on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now please turn to paragraph 63 of your statement. That's page 11 in English and in your version it's page 17. Here you speak of Basara and the 6th Brigade. There are various assessments, but let's say that there were about 3.000 members of that 6th Brigade. That number used to vary but it went from 3- to 5.000; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 63 when you met with Basara I see that this brigade was deployed - and this is something you spoke of yesterday - that they had their positions. And when you visited him you said that that brigade was quartered on a large piece of land. Was it in Lusci Palanka, were they there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were from Palanka over across Dabar in an area stretching over 30 kilometres. This is where they were positioned, and one couldn't see them from the road, either from the regional road or the local road. One couldn't see them because they were out in the hills where they had their camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 65 of your statement, when speaking of the numbers of the SOS, you say that in your estimate there were between 38 and 40 persons there. Can you confirm that now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you say that Dusko Saovic, nicknamed Njunja, was the commander of that group. Tell me, please, this Njunja person, did he come to the meetings of the Crisis Staff? Did he take part in political activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither he nor -- it's just that when the Crisis Staff was established, Vinko Nikolic from the SOS was their representative at the Crisis Staff. And up until that time they never appeared in such meetings, and none of them were members of the Executive Board of the SDS even though some of them were most likely members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. And then in paragraph 66 you speak of how from the fall of 1991 until spring of 1992 there were about 13 instances of grenades being thrown on certain premises, most likely owned by Muslims and Croats. And then you say that there were probably some damage inflicted on premises owned by Serbs as well. And you testified of that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 2D02-0441, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is the document that we looked at the other day, Mr. Majkic. Unfortunately, I don't have it in our language, but I will read out to you several excerpts to remind you of what it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you leave this statement that you have been cross-examining the witness on, I understand this is not yet exhibited. Do you wish to have it exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I have a couple more issues to cover regarding this statement, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So you're coming back to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am coming back, but in fact it's not my intention -- I just want to point -- to make several points with that regard. I just want to know what's going on with this particular document that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TULLY
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, the number is 2D02-0440.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this document will be shown on the screen, the translation, but let me tell you what it is about. This is a daily report on the visit of the Red Cross delegation from Sarajevo on the 24th of February, 1992, and their representatives talked to Nedeljko Rasula from SDS, to Mirzet Karabeg, president of the Executive Board, member of the SDA; they talked to Ivica Pranic, the HDZ representative, which is the Croatian political party; and Majkic Dragan. You see the names here in English. Do you remember even though it was 17 years ago. Do you remember that meeting with the representatives of the Red Cross in February of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there was the meeting, but I can't remember the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Naturally. I didn't insist on them, but this is the document. It is self-explanatory, and we will go over it. So briefly in this document they describe the situation in the municipality. They say that there are about 2.000 refugees. I suppose that these refugees are Serbs who had come from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Then they go on to say that there are about 5.000 unemployed persons in -- briefly, the economic situation was difficult. You had to take care of the refugees, deal with the unemployment, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly. I just wondered whose report is it. It's a report made by the ICRC, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Majkic, they say here in the fourth paragraph from the bottom that from November 1991 there had been about 20 explosions in cafes, bars, and cars, and they say that they were not focused exclusively on one ethnicity but on all three of them. Would you agree with this conclusion of the Red Cross delegation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we turn to the second page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph it says that the team received a confirmation from all three political leaders in Sanski Most, that all three ethnic groups were armed, and that nobody felt threatened on account of that. As I see it, they simply took it as a given fact. This was the period of time just before the outbreak of the war and this is what these people from the Red Cross stated; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there is no objection from my friends from Prosecution, we could mark it for identification pending translation if it's possible. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D19, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Or, Your Honours, sorry, if we don't need translation, if this is original document, we could have it marked as an exhibit. I don't know what's the practice. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked as an exhibit, and I assume that the procedure would be followed to have it translated into the language that the accused understands in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now let us turn to paragraph 111. That's page 18 in the English version and page 28 in the Serbian. You say there that since you were replaced or following your replacement - and this is what you said to the OTP as well - that you knew that people were brought in, their statements taken, and so on, in certain places. And then in paragraph 111 you say that one could see that there were people in prison there and that everybody knew that and that it was even broadcast on the radio. So if you knew that and if this was a relatively well-known fact, does it mean that the public prosecutor in Sanski Most had to know of this too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, this did not refer to the people who were arrested and brought to the hall. This referred to the people who lived in that neighbourhood called Mahala. After the 27th, when the military operation in Mahala was carried out, on the following day they all came out of that neighbourhood and spread, dispersed throughout the city. And then several days later when somebody issued a decision, they went through Mahala, the entire town going door to door looking for people from Mahala. And having found those from Mahala, they took them to the sports hall where they were kept for several days, and then via Bosanska Krupa they were transported in the direction of Cazin. This here refers to that particular group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understood this to mean that the position of the public prosecutor in Sanski Most was such that he had information on certain aspects that could be prosecuted -- that people could be prosecuted for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, let us discuss -- let us turn to the document that you discussed yesterday which is the purported diary. This is a contentious issue still, the diary of Rasula, which is P60.13. All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please. Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, my microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us turn to page where we see the entry for the 2nd of November, or rather, we go to the 2nd of November page of the diary where the meeting held on the 20th of April is recorded. So we should see the 2nd of November. Right now we see the 22nd of October which is no good for us. We need to move forward. I can assist you. This is page with the ERN number 0037-9441, so 20 some numbers further along. MR. DI FAZIO: I might have missed it. Do we have the English corresponding page?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the page. The English version ... in the English version we need to find the 18th of April, 1992, and the 20th of April, 1992. While our colleagues from the Registry are looking for it -- could we now scroll down in the English version so we can see the entire text -- or rather, can we see the top of the page, the 18th of April. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is the meeting held on the 20th of April, 1992, where General Talic, Colonel Basara, Major Zeljaja were present, as well as representatives of the SDS, SDA, and HDZ, also attending were Mirzet, Redzo, Sabic, Ante, and Vlado. This is for the record. General Talic was actually commander of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara was the commander of the 6th Brigade in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, Major Zelja ja was a commander of some military brigade in the region of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two brigades in Prijedor. One was motorised and I don't know what the other one was, and he was a commander of one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what I know is that Major Zeljaja was at the same level as Colonel Basara. He was in charge of all military forces in the area of Prijedor, just like Basara was in Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had a brigade under his command or a battalion. It's possible that he had a brigade under his command, in which case he held the same position in Prijedor as did Basara in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And there were representatives of all political parties there. Now tell me, Mirzet, is that Mirzet Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, president of the municipal Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who was Redzo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Redzo Kurbegovic was either president of the SDA at the time. He may have been president of the SDA at the time; if not exactly president, then one of the top leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about Sabic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Suad Sabic was a lawyer before the war and he was vice-president of the SDA in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who is Ante?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante was president of the HDZ in Sanski Most. I can't remember his last name just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Vlado, was that Vlado Vrkes from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vlado Vrkes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On that day, military leaders, together with political leaders, agreed on and analysed the situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know about this meeting at all at the time. I only learned of it many years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. Now, see here on this page it says Redzo and then the text that is attributed to him. And Redzo is reading some political party communique. I assume it was a joint one from all political parties on how to reach some peaceful resolution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I didn't know of this meeting, but reading this text one could come to that conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And we have a sentence here. Redzo gives a consent for this division -- these divisions to be made in the municipality, which means that there was some political agreement on carrying out divisions based on ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if this was on the 20th this could be the continuation of the negotiations held on the 15th and the 16th. I don't know what else it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then Redzo speaks of some agreement on five items. He doesn't agree with the time schedule for moving out, but he advocates the position that the facility needs to be handed over peacefully. I guess he speaks of the facility that belonged to the police; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really couldn't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us now move to the following page, which is the 3rd of November, so the same meeting. It is carried over onto the next page, and see here what Ante says. He was the representative of the Croatian political party. Ante says that he doesn't accept the opinion of the headquarters of the HDZ, so he's opposed to it. And then Ante says that the Croat population - and then he speaks of the relations between these two peoples and how they have no power in the municipality. And then Ante approves the idea of Serbian municipality, and is awaiting some response from Sarajevo. And Ante is appealing to the army to preserve law and order. Did you know this Ante personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: His words here, do they faithfully reflect the position of the HDZ in Sanski Most, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't [as interpreted] tell you one specific thing about this. At that time at the Assembly, only one vote was missing for the Assembly to adopt the decision to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And in talks with the SDS, Ante accepted to give that missing vote. However, at the last moment he changed his mind and didn't vote for it. And as soon as I came back to Sanski Most I met up with this Ante. We sat down and talked about it, and after the war, sometime in 2000, he told me that he had been willing to vote but he changed his mind at the last moment in fear of Tudjman in Zagreb. He said, "I was quite willing but I didn't dare."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's just correct this first sentence. There's a mistake on the record, page 20, line 3. We heard you saying "I can tell you one specific thing about this." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Minor correction. Never mind. So there was a political negotiation in Sanski Most. Representatives of the military were involved as well as higher political leaderships, that is, the headquarters of these political parties, and there was a great drive to resolve the situation in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could infer that from all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned yesterday that the essence of this division lay both in the structure of the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the structure of the municipal police; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it also had to do with the territory of Sanski Most itself. You even said that one part of the town would go to the Serbian people, another part to the Muslim people, a third part to the Croats. Did I understand this well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those talks they divided the entire territory of Sanski Most and marked each section and who's going to control it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now we are moving to another subject that had been discussed yesterday, namely, according to you, Mr. Zupljanin always tried to be tolerant and professional in seeking solutions so that this transformation of the police and the division of the police would take place in a civilised way. We will now see a video-clip that the Prosecution used in its opening statement. Of course the Prosecution is entitled to certain interpretations, just as the Defence does. And the final decision will be made by the Trial Chamber. So could we now look at this excerpt in which Mr. Zupljanin in an interview speaks of the manner, kind, and structure of the organisation of the Serbian police, and then I will put certain questions to you regarding that. Unfortunately, we have no translation, and I am kindly asking the interpreters now to interpret the interview as best they can. I was told that perhaps this translation would be provided by the translation section, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 3008. [In English] Can we play this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "To take off the uniform and be a regular person. "I set this as an objective when I decided with a couple of my colleagues to work intensively on preparations that preceded the war on the one hand aware of the threats to the Serbian populace. It is my great desire to create a police force in the right measure for the -- for the people. Our example we are following are the English bobbies. We believe that they are held in great respect by their own people, that it's an honour for an English citizen when a policeman comes to his house. And above all, this is a well-trained professional, a moral man. When I say 'moral,' it's quite certain that in our previous system morals were eroded greatly. I must say that it is the same with personal ethics. I remember times when I was able to find time to read. I took Aristotle's politics, and I underlined one of his thoughts when he said that the most important task of the state is to preserve morals. I believe our state must do a lot in this respect in the following period. "Speaking of the police, it's quite certain that we must adopt into the police force the most faithful young people with clean hands and clear minds who are not interested only in money, but who are prepared to give their best and even lay down their lives for the welfare of their people."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, do you remember, do you agree that in those times when you worked with Mr. Zupljanin he was really trying to achieve a high level of professionalism in the police force in the entire region covered by the CSB Banja Luka in the spirit of his words here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not seen this clip before, but I am 100 per cent certain from what I know of Mr. Zupljanin that what he said here in this video-clip, that was precisely his idea in the times when I was working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you. [In English] Sorry, maybe I can tender it as an exhibit, this video-clip, if there is no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- finally it was part of the opening statement. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Majkic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D20, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Majkic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you the questions I plan to ask, could we call up on the screen one document that you commented on yesterday, it's been exhibited, P355. As we are waiting, let me tell you that you won't be asked to comment on it again - you did that yesterday - but I need it as a reminder to you for the question that follows. Those are the conclusions of that meeting of 6 April 1992. Just remind yourself of the introductory part that begins with the words: "In accordance with the current political developments in the republic resulting from the problems that had occurred with the future state organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the fundamental principles of which were established by the Sarajevo agreement and confirmed by the Brussels recognition," et cetera, et cetera. You remember this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Read also the following passage, the next passage. It speaks about the establishment of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian republic. You remember seeing this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to page 2. Excellent. Let's find the English. It begins with: "In this connection" or "on that occasion ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Read this as well. "On that occasion and in accordance with dispatch of the MUP collegium of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 2nd of April, 1992, on the need for internal affairs organs to be transformed ..." Could we just put it the way I said it in the record. "In accordance with the SRBH MUP collegium dispatch" - I wanted this acronym on the record because it had caused some misunderstanding earlier. Have you read it now? "On the transformation of internal affairs organs and their security services that should be carried out in a peaceful manner and without excess situations."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now this acronym, SRBH, I believe my colleague Mr. Pantelic mentioned it yesterday. SRBH as an acronym can be read in our language as Serbian Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it can also be read as Socialist Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Pantelic said that this was a dispatch of the MUP collegium of the Serbian Republic B&H; however, I'll also remind you and we'll refer to the document, at that time, on the 2nd of April, the MUP of Republika Srpska only has ministers, Minister Jovica [as interpreted] Stanisic. It does not have a collegium. The first time the collegium met was in July in Belgrade. Correction to the transcript, Mico Stanisic, not Jovica Stanisic. So reference was made to the dispatch of the MUP collegium of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the collegium of a joint MUP, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since this document is already in evidence, the only way to check if what I'm saying is correct is to open this dispatch and look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if we should do that before the break. Maybe I'll take some time reading it, but I don't mind continuing if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we have about seven minutes -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's make as much use of the time as we have. We have about seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we now open 65 ter 2768. Could we just zoom in a bit. First show the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, we have to start from the very beginning. Look, MUP, Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It says dispatch number, official, and the date. And then it lists the addressees; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's clearly written there. We don't need to read it out, but we see that there are many bodies among the addressees.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, down to the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But also the federal secretariat of internal affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And look, who follows after the federal secretariat, Minister -- Ministers of internal affairs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course I wouldn't presume to tell you how to conduct your cross-examination, but these prefatory questions, I for one am at a loss as to where you're headed. Perhaps it would be of greater assistance to the witness and the Chamber if you were to hone in on the end of that road down which you're headed. It's a mixed metaphor, but pardon me. You understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, will you then read the beginning of the first paragraph of the conclusions from this joint collegium.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it similar or identical to what we've just seen in the dispatch from Mr. Zupljanin; you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You'll agree with me that that paragraph was practically copied and pasted by Mr. Zupljanin or he just gave his own account of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Look at that same first paragraph, there is this notification of the establishment of the Ministry of the Interior of the republic of the Serbian people Bosnia-Herzegovina; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that written?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Mr. Zupljanin copied and pasted this as well into his own dispatch, we've just seen it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now look, it says "page 2" in the middle of the page, so could we just see the lower part. Are we there in the English version? Yeah, there it is. It's difficult to count the lines, but somewhere in the middle the sentence begins: "The professional collegium made an appraisal of the situation realistically and -- having realistically reviewed the prevailing situation and wanting to avoid the conditions possible for further deterioration of an otherwise complex situation with the intention to maintain the control over all elements of law and order, particularly when it comes to personal security of the citizens and their property."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, find this sentence that begins with the words "collegium" and read on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When you reach a convenient point we'll take the break, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll finish with this document before the break, and after the break we'll discuss an entirely different subject if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you find it verbatim as I read it out? I'll remind you -- you need look at the document no longer. I'll remind you that Mr. Zupljanin in his dispatch mentions this very same thing, "peacefully and without incident and excesses." You agree that Mr. Zupljanin is referring to this dispatch? He actually gave his own account of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question on this for the witness, but maybe I should ask it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, while the witness is on his way back to the stand, for management purposes because as you would be aware there are a number of other matters with which we must deal with today, including a witness who is standing by in Belgrade for the videolink. Could you give us an indication as to how much longer you expect you would be with this witness? We recall that when -- that the usual order for cross-examination was reversed because you anticipated at the end of examination-in-chief that the witness's testimony being matters that concern the -- Mr. Zupljanin more so than Mr. Stanisic, that you would, as it was, sweep up after Mr. Pantelic would have done the -- I keep mixing metaphors, but the heavy lifting in terms of the cross-examination. So now that you have had the benefit of Mr. Pantelic's work, could you tell us now where you think you are in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you are quite right. I'm not going to repeat what Mr. Pantelic has already covered, and I will deal only with matters that I believe to be important for the defence of Mr. Stanisic. I told my learned friends from the Prosecution that I will not be as long as until the next break, and as to exactly how long I wouldn't be able to tell you. Perhaps I'll finish in the next half an hour, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. Just for the record I would like to ask just a correction for the exhibit 2D20 -- actually, it is a videotape I was informed during the break of two and a half hours. So just for the record I would need a clip of this whole tape from minute 1 -- hour 1, 57 minute, and 20 seconds up to hour 1, 59 minutes, and 35 seconds, just this particular portion. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the Registry will deal with that in the usual manner. Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, now that we're dealing with this page of this document, would you please look at the text below that where it says: "Also due attention was paid to the financing," and so on. Were you able to find it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can see that in the English version as well. Have you read the entire paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the collegium of the joint Ministry of the Interior is here dealing also with the issue of the funding and financing of the Ministry of the Interior, and they accepted as a fact that the Ministry of the Interior does indeed exist. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that at the end they are mentioning the possibility of maintaining some joint services. Do you see that bit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We have the acronym EOP here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think that EOP stands for electronic data processing and communications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the top echelons of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is here dealing with the transformation and reorganisation of the MUP; am I right, this is what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you realise that in this particular instance the reference is made to the reorganisation of the existing structure of the ministry -- I apologise, I'm now being told that you need to wait with your answer to be sure that it was properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will have to repeat the question. I will have to repeat the question. So do you agree that the collegium of the joint Ministry of the Interior here deals with the existence funding of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian republic and also speaks how some joint services within the joint MUP should be maintained; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: They are referring to the electronic data processing, communications system, and so on; right? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could I ask the Registry to go back to the first page of this document. We need to see the English version as well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Majkic, as it happens, you were a member both of the joint MUP and a member of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please read paragraph 2 where it says who attended the professional collegium of the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The list is quite lengthy so you needed additional time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you? There was something I wanted to ask you. So you know all of these people, the names are familiar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, back from the times of the joint MUP where we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you can confirm that they actually performed the duties and served in the posts that are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that these were indeed the top officials of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, practically all of them except for Alija Delimustafic, whose name for some reason I can't see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And everybody else is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I would like to tender this document into evidence because it is evident that the contents of this document are incorporated into the contents of the dispatch that we admitted yesterday into evidence as P355, dispatch of Mr. Zupljanin who actually used the conclusions reached at the joint collegium and incorporated them into his dispatch. We believe this document to be very important, this document here, and we believe that this document can be used to explain the one that was admitted yesterday, and that they should be only analysed together in order to explain the procedure for reorganisation of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, please explain to the Chamber the importance of the fact that Mr. Zupljanin copied a part of the joint MUP meeting conclusions into his own dispatch. What are we to make of this? What do you seek to prove by having this established?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to show how the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina was transformed, along which lines; what hierarchy existed and how it went down; I'm also trying to show the fact that this transformation came about based on the consent of all three sides, representative of all three nations, who were represented among the top officials of MUP. I asked the witness to look at the list of attendees - and I can repeat my question and ask him whether all three nations, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims were represented among the attendees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's clear that they were. I -- as I said, I knew most of them and I used to meet with almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. But again, Mr. Cvijetic, what is the importance of the fact in relation to the -- to this trial, what is the importance of the fact that the transformation was done through negotiation between the three parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm following the indictment. According to the indictment, MUP or Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska was created by force, by taking over power by force, by splitting. However, as we can see based on this document, we can -- this came about based on the political agreement, the Lisbon Agreement, Cutileiro Plan, and so on, and that the policemen up until that time simply followed the agreement that was reached at the political level among the representatives of all three nations. So that is the essence of what I'm trying to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D78, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, you have heard the reply I gave to the Trial Chamber, so let's deal with that context, please. You were there on the ground, and as you have told us you were there awaiting the results of the political discussions of all three nations in order to see what you, policemen, were to do. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will then agree with my conclusion, won't you, that you - the policemen - if I may say so, were waiting to see what fate will be cut out for you by the politicians and that the politics came above everything else; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, I will now go to the very beginning when you were appointed chief in Sanski Most. You said something and I have it in your statement used by Mr. Pantelic, that you were nominated for that post by the Serbian Democratic Party, but that your nomination was approved by other ethnic political -- by political parties of other ethnicities; and that it was only after the consent was given by them that you were officially appointed to that post. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D00-7018. We are waiting for the translation of this document into English. It should be ready tomorrow. Therefore, I will simply ask the witness to confirm and to read out to the interpreters the heading of the document so that the interpreters can interpret for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you please read it but slowly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbian Democratic Party Bosnia and Herzegovina. Municipal Board in Sanski Most number 28/91, date 29th of April, 1991. "Heading: To the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you read the first sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We kindly ask that based on the inter-party agreement of the SDS branch in Sanski Most and the Party of Democratic Action of Sanski Most, we ask you to request consent from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina for appointment of the chief of the public security station in Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now stop there. We see that your personal details are -- come after that. We don't need to go over them. It would take too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we please turn to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can see here personal details of another two candidates, and would you please read the last sentence at the very bottom where it says: "We kindly ask ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We kindly ask that based on the agreement between the SDA and SDS of Sanski Most, you give priority to the candidate under number 1, Dragan Majkic."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And on the left side we see the stamp of the SDA party and on the right-hand side we see the stamp of the SDS party. So is this what you spoke about, about you receiving approval from other political parties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we mark this document for identification, and I do have the promise given by the CLSS that the translation would be ready tomorrow, and since the witness has recognised, so to speak, his own nomination in this document then could we MFI it until we receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D79, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Majkic, let me remind you of your own words. Regardless of who nominated you, your duty was to work in the interest of all nations. Did I interpret your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you then, due to that, if I may say so, freeze or put on hold your political work within the secretariat of the Serbian Democratic Party? And I will put to you what you said in paragraph 28 of your statement where you said: "This meeting was held after I had been appointed chief of police in Sanski Most ..." And then you say: "I did not attend the meeting. As a professional policeman I did not wish to be seen as somebody who was politically active." Now, my question for you is this: This attitude of yours, does it arise from a broader view that prosecutors, policemen, and so on cannot be politically active while in office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, you will agree with me, won't you, that police work is universal throughout the world. My colleague mentioned an English bobby, policeman, who has one kind of uniform; Italian Carabinieri have different uniforms; French Gendarmes have yet another uniform, but all of them carry out a similar kind of work; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So regardless of the uniform and symbols -- so regardless of the uniform and symbols, your work is basically the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will then ask you to read -- to look at and read a document that has been translated, 65 ter 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian it's page 5. In the English version it's page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is the Law on Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1990, Article 41.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the year of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you're asked to repeat the year of the law, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. It was 1990. Do we have Article 41? We need the end of that article that begin with the words "authorised officials."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Majkic, would you please start reading out the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean "authorised officials"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Authorised officials have the right and the duty" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. The third paragraph from the bottom starts with the same words, with the same words "authorised officials."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Authorised officials have" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, no, underneath.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. "Authorised officials give a solemn declaration before the republic secretary or an official authorised by him."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text of the solemn declaration reads: "I declare that I will perform the duties of an authorised official conscientiously and responsibly, that I will abide by the constitution and the law, and that I will protect with all my power the constitutionally determined system, the rights, freedoms, and safety of working people and citizens, and that I will perform these and other jobs and tasks of an authorised official, even in the cases when their execution may put my life in danger."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the text of the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this is from the time when you yourself were a policeman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now is the good time to compare the translation of the term "solemn declaration." I think that in the translation we see the word "oath" if I'm not mistaken, whereas in the original in the Serbian, as the witness has read out, it says "solemn declaration." We will request that Article 41 of the English version of this law be changed and sent to the CLSS translation service in order to be corrected so that it corresponds to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we took Mr. Zecevic's point on that on Friday and the matter was referred to CLSS, so it's not anything that the Chamber can do. We fully understand the problem and the -- Mr. Zecevic's observations in which inferentially the Prosecution have concurred all a matter of record now. I don't know that there is anything further that the Chamber could or indeed do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I took note of that. Our intervention was duly recorded in the transcript. So these different formulations will need to be changed, and the reason why I showed this text to the witness is of a different nature. I'm leading witness to that and we will get to that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now Mr. Zecevic is telling me that this is a different document, not the one on account of which he intervened the other day, and this is why we ask that this document also be corrected by the translation service. So that's what I wanted to say on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's a problem with the document that's presently before us? Oh, I see. Again, the -- this will be married to the -- what we said on Friday would be sorted out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, in the text of this solemn declaration, you see the words "protect the constitutionally determined system." See that word?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And then it says "the rights, freedoms, and safety of working people and citizens ..." so remember these two words "system" and the rights, freedoms, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see document 65 ter 53, please, which is the Law on the Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska from 1992. We need page 6 in the B/C/S version and page 9 in the English version. As it happens, we need the same article, 41. The lower part, please, with the reference to the solemn declaration. Yes, that one. In English as well -- oh, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, you've already heard what is on the screen. You don't have to read it aloud this time, this last paragraph which says that authorised officials shall make a solemn declaration. Just read it to yourself and then I'll ask my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: While you're reading, this English version refers to a formal statement. Obviously this is a third translation that again has to be harmonised with the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, is your purpose of bringing these documents to this witness to have the translation issue settled? Because if so, then I suggest that we -- you can just do it directly without having to go through a witness. Mind you, your half-hour is almost up and we have a witness waiting in Sarajevo I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was not my intention to correct the translations now while the witness is reading. I just wanted to draw your attention to the reason why we keep intervening about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, have you read it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you make notes of the two words that I asked you to pay attention to? They're not in the text, "working people" and "citizens." That's not in the text. It only says "rights, freedoms, and security." These are very general terms without any reference to working people and citizens.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree that this term, "working people and citizens," is a relic or a remnant from the previous communist terminology, and that's why it was omitted probably. And instead of the word "order" or "system" we see "the established arrangement of the republic, the established order of the republic." Let me ask you -- let me not say everywhere in the world, but in Europe, wherever there are republics, would it be the same formulation or in every region of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every policeman who read this would accept and sign something like this without thinking long. In Capljina where I worked, for instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, tell us where Capljina was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Herzegovina, under Croat control.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if I were from Capljina I would sign this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So a policeman who wants to be an authorised official and is not prepared to fight for the values enshrined in this solemn declaration is practically unable to perform his duties because this is his legal obligation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you entered the courtroom, the first document you were shown was the text of the solemn declaration; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you accepted it. It is then a logical conclusion that you want to be a witness and that you are prepared to speak only the truth. You remember the text of the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If you had not accepted, we would have to infer the opposite, that you don't want to be a witness and you don't want to speak the truth; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, the only other thing I want to deal with is the termination of your job. Yesterday you were shown a document, conclusion of the crisis of the 30th of April, 1992. You said you were present at the time when the item of the agenda was discussed or related to your replacement by Mirko Vrucinic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had invited me --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just be brief.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had invited me to that meeting just to inform me that I was replaced and that Mirko was taking over and that a solution should be found as to where I would work next, whether in the police or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at one document 1D00-6759. There it is. Mr. Majkic, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff not only adopted the decision, but also drafted an official appointment for Mirko Vrucinic. You are a policeman and you know the format of appointment to important jobs in the police. You will agree with me that this is not the proper way. This is a different way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This decision of the Crisis Staff, nevertheless, took effect. Mr. Vrucinic took over, assumed the job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Does this confirm that at that time Crisis Staff were the main authority at the local and regional level alike?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only -- not only the most important but the only authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, Sanski Most after the Dayton Accords remained within the territory of the Federation, that is, outside Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A smaller part which is now the municipality Ostra Luka remained within Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that a settlement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But the main part of Sanski Most remained within the Federation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the greatest part of what used to be the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Help me now, you said you went back to work in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2nd October 2000 was the day when I started to work in the MUP, the cantonal MUP of Bihac, that was the base. I just had an office in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were working, your report on fire protection was made from that post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were later abolished because until that time we had dual authority, as an inspectorate and as authorised officials. In 2003 the powers of police were abolished as far as we were concerned, and we remained an inspection authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There, in the police force, they wear different uniforms and different emblems. We discussed that yesterday; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were not bothered by working among such colleagues wearing that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't mind. If I did, I wouldn't have returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were chief in Sanski Most, that's when this transformation happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: After you stopped being chief, you continued to work in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Betonirka, Krings Hall, and the sports hall, Manjaca were mentioned here. You were not afraid of going back to Sanski Most to be among Muslims and Croats, despite what I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had been afraid, I wouldn't have returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you did not feel you were responsible for any of those things, so you did not fear coming back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to tender document 1D00-6759, and that's the appointment -- the document appointing Mr. Mirko Vrucinic as chief of the public security station. The witness is aware of this document, and I would like to tender it. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D80, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one more question before I finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, after you were no longer chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go on? Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So after you were no longer chief, you continued to work at the public security station of Sanski Most and you were doing your job, which is fire protection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned after about a year to those -- to that job in CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Until when did you remain in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to go out to on-site investigations in cases of explosions, fires, et cetera, in 1993 -- sorry, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two cases when although I was not the fire inspector the crimes involved fires and other criminal acts, and investigators asked me, investigators from the public security station of Sanski Most, asked me to go help investigate the crime scene. I know that on two occasions I went in case of fire. One case was in Kamengrad and one former policeman of ours, a Muslim, was injured. Zdravko Savanovic and I both detected and apprehended the perpetrators within 24 hours and turned the perpetrator over to the public prosecutor. Another case happened in Naprelje village, there was a fire and looting.
